title: Fisher–Yates shuffle
text:
The modern version of the Fisher–Yates shuffle, designed for computer use, was introduced by Richard Durstenfeld in 1964[1] and popularized by Donald E. Knuth in The Art of Computer Programming as "Algorithm P (Shuffling)".[2] Neither Durstenfeld's article nor Knuth's first edition of The Art of Computer Programming acknowledged the work of Fisher and Yates. Subsequent editions of Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming mention Fisher and Yates' contribution.[3]

The algorithm described by Durstenfeld is more efficient than that given by Fisher and Yates: whereas a naïve computer implementation of Fisher and Yates' method would spend needless time counting the remaining numbers in step 3 above, Durstenfeld's solution is to move the "struck" numbers to the end of the list by swapping them with the last unstruck number at each iteration. This reduces the algorithm's time complexity to O(n) compared to O(n^2) for the naïve implementation.[4] This change gives the following algorithm (for a zero-based array).

-- To shuffle an array a of n elements (indices 0..n − 1):

for i from n − 1 down to 1 do

j ← random integer such that 0 ≤ j ≤ i

exchange a[j] and a[i]

An equivalent version which shuffles the array in the opposite direction (from lowest index to highest) is:

for i from 0 to n − 2 do

j ← random integer such that i ≤ j ≤ n − 1

exchange a[i] and a[j]

Since the inverse of a uniformly random permutation is uniformly random, one can equally well perform the loops above in the other direction:

for i from 1 to n − 1 do

j ← random integer such that 0 ≤ j ≤ i

exchange a[j] and a[i]

Or:

for i from n − 2 down to 0 do

j ← random integer such that i ≤ j ≤ n − 1

exchange a[i] and a[j]
